caption_hook: Virginia has been a shell-filled seafloor, a coal swamp and the roots of an ancient mountain chain.

layers.name: YORKTOWN FORMATION
layers.hook: A warm sea packed with shells
layers.what: Not long ago in geologic terms, a warm shallow sea covered eastern Virginia. Its shells, shark teeth and sand settled into the Yorktown Formation, which lines river banks near the Chesapeake Bay.
layers.bonus: A fossil scallop from this layer, Chesapecten, is Virginia's official state fossil.

layers.name: POCAHONTAS FORMATION
layers.what: Giant ferns and scale trees grew in steamy coastal swamps. Buried and squeezed for millions of years, they became the thick coal seams of Virginia's far southwest.
layers.bonus: The Pocahontas Exhibition Mine lets visitors walk inside the old coal workings.

layers.name: MASSANUTTEN SANDSTONE
layers.hook: Ancient beach sand, now a ridge
layers.what: Rivers and shorelines spread clean sand across the region long before the dinosaurs. Pressed into tough sandstone, it now caps a long ridge in the middle of the Shenandoah Valley.
layers.bonus: Massanutten Mountain is a 50-mile ridge that splits the valley's river in two.

layers.name: CATOCTIN FORMATION
layers.what: When an ancient supercontinent tore apart, lava poured across the land in huge floods. Later baked and squeezed, it became the green-tinged rock that forms the high Blue Ridge crest.
layers.bonus: Hawksbill, the tallest peak in Shenandoah National Park at 4,051 ft, is capped by it.

layers.name: OLD RAG GRANITE
layers.hook: The roots of a lost mountain range
layers.what: Over a billion years ago, molten rock cooled deep underground during a continental collision. Millions of years of erosion have exposed it as the rounded, boulder-strewn summit of Old Rag.
layers.bonus: Old Rag's rock scramble is one of the most-hiked trails in Virginia.
